summary:
Ghost Rovers is an interactive 3D web experience that brings NASA’s retired and abandoned hardware back to life for school-age space fans. Students spin a realistic globe of the Moon or Mars, or explore a Deep Space gallery, and click glowing icons that mark where each machine still sits today, from Apollo’s Eagle and the Moon buggies to Sojourner, Opportunity, Viking, and Ingenuity.

Each machine tells its own story in the first person, in short, easy steps with real NASA photos. Instead of long text, every card shows a status badge (resting, quiet, or lost contact) and a simple number or chart, such as Opportunity’s planned 90 days versus its actual 15 years of work.

The project answers the challenge by turning dense mission data into a personal story that connects each machine’s engineering to the science it made possible. It matters because these robotic explorers paved the way for today’s missions, yet students rarely hear about them. Built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Globe.gl, it runs in any browser with no installation.
details:
What it does / how it works: Ghost Rovers is an interactive 3D web experience about the hardware NASA left behind. Users choose Moon, Mars, or Deep Space. On the Moon and Mars, they drag to spin a realistic globe and click glowing icons placed at each machine’s real landing site (Apollo’s Eagle, three Moon buggies, Surveyor landers, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Viking, Phoenix, InSight, Ingenuity). Deep Space probes (Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer 10 and 11, Kepler) appear in their own gallery, since they are not on either world. Clicking an icon flies the globe to the site and opens a card with real NASA photos and a short first-person story told step by step with Back/Next buttons. Each card also shows a status badge (resting, quiet, or lost contact) and a simple number or bar chart, such as Opportunity’s planned 90 days versus its actual 15 years, plus a link to the NASA mission page.

Benefits and intended impact: Students learn through exploring, not reading long text. Photos, numbers, and short stories make complex mission history easy to grasp. We hope students feel a personal connection to these robotic explorers and see how past missions made today’s discoveries possible.

Tools: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript; Globe.gl (built on Three.js) for the 3D globes; VS Code and Live Server for development. Data and images come from NASA NSSDCA, science.nasa.gov mission pages, and the NASA Image and Video Library, with globe textures based on NASA lunar and Mars mapping data. No special hardware is needed, and it runs in any modern browser.

Creativity: The machines speak in their own voices, and the “ghost rover” idea turns forgotten hardware into characters worth meeting.

Factors we considered: Young audience (short text, big visuals), accuracy (facts checked against NASA mission pages), and accessibility (no installation, works on any device with a browser).
dataRefs: NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA)
